text: You're signing into Spotify, but you enter the wrong password.
Should the app open because you were close?
Or maybe because your spelling was creative?
No.
You want it to follow a strict rule.
Let me in only if the password matches exactly.
Traditional, non-AI software is built entirely on these kinds of explicit instructions written
by people.
Whether it's a calculator performing math or a spreadsheet applying formulas, it does
exactly what it's told.
This flowchart shows what those rules look like.
The process starts at the top node, waiting for a password.
At the if condition, matching data flows to the then action, opening the app.
If it fails, the else action triggers an error.
Written rules are absolutely reliable.
Now imagine a messy, handwritten homecoming playlist with crossed out ideas, arrows,
abbreviations, and jokes.
Before using this list, you must decode it.
If a programmer tried writing an if-then rule for every random scribble, it would be impossible.
Traditional software fails here.
This is where artificial intelligence becomes useful.
An LLM learns patterns during training.
By relying on learned patterns rather than strict instructions, AI makes sense of messy
notes, organizing them into a clean, usable list.
But there is no magic happening behind the screen.
AI is still software.
Human developers still write the core code that trains and runs the system.
The key difference is that they have stopped writing a separate, explicit rule for every
single possible user request.
When scenarios become too complex to predict, software must shift from executing rigid commands
to interpreting learned patterns to actually produce a usable result.
Here's a cooking analogy.
Role-based software is a cooking robot.
A human wrote the recipe, and the robot blindly repeats it for the exact same result.
AI is an experienced chef.
Operating on learned patterns, the chef recognizes pairings and substitutions without a recipe,
allowing for new, unexpected dishes.
To calculate a GPA, you put grades into specific rows and columns.
That is structured data, information organized into consistent fields.
Compare that to a campus photograph.
The visual information isn't arranged in fields.
This is unstructured data.
AI uses visual context to identify dorm buildings without a neat grid.
There is a trade-off, however.
While learned patterns make AI incredibly flexible with unstructured data, this same
trait makes its responses much harder to inspect or predict, compared to that strict
password rule we saw earlier.
Because it isn't following exact rules, the AI might miss a crossed-out song on
your playlist, or it might confidently hallucinate the wrong dorm name.
It might look great, but still have mistakes.
Ultimately, neither system is universally superior.
They are simply distinct instruments designed for different types of problems.
Different jobs need different tools.
Choose the tool that fits the work.
